title: Exponentially hard weak versus strong one-way functions
formal: Does the existence of an exponentially hard weak one-way function imply the existence of an exponentially hard strong one-way function, in the following nonuniform-adversary, negligible-success formulation? The premise is that there exist a uniform polynomial-time computable length-preserving function \(f\), a real \(a>0\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and \(n_0\), such that \[\operatorname{Inv}_f(C,n)\le1-n^{-k}\] for every \(n\ge n_0\) and every circuit \(C\) with \(n\) inputs, \(n\) outputs and at most \(2^{an}\) gates. The desired conclusion is that there exist another uniform polynomial-time computable length-preserving function \(g\) and a real \(b>0\) such that, for every integer \(d\ge1\), there is \(n_d\) with \[\operatorname{Inv}_g(C,n)\le n^{-d}\] for every \(n\ge n_d\) and every such circuit with at most \(2^{bn}\) gates. The constants and function in the conclusion may depend on those witnessing the premise.
why: Ordinary hardness amplification equates weak and strong one-wayness at polynomial security scales. Preserving hardness exponential in the actual input length would extend that equivalence to a much stronger regime and clarify how fine-grained average-case hardness supports cryptographic security.
status_note: The 2021 source and its 25 August 2025 revision explicitly leave exponential weak-to-strong amplification open. Checked on 2026-09-14, together with the regular-function amplification source and a bounded later-work search. The card states the nonuniform, length-preserving, negligible-success convention explicitly; no exhaustive current-status certification is claimed.

importance.reason: A foundational hardness-amplification question separating ordinary cryptographic equivalences from security exponential in input length, with direct connections to average-case hardness and meta-complexity.

sentences: The premise is a polynomial-time function that defeats exponential-size inversion circuits on an inverse-polynomial fraction of inputs.
The question asks whether this already guarantees a function whose inversion success is negligible for exponential-size circuits.
An attacker succeeds by finding any preimage of a challenge sampled from a uniform input.
Ordinary repetition enlarges the input and can lose hardness exponential in the new length.
Security-preserving results for regular functions do not settle the general case, which remains open in a 2025 revision.

definitions:
A length-preserving function is a single map \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) with \(|f(x)|=|x|\), computed by one deterministic multitape Turing machine in at most \(A(n+1)^r\) steps on every input of length \(n\), for some fixed constants \(A,r\). The same convention applies to \(g\). There is no oracle or advice in forward evaluation.

For a circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^n\), define its inversion success by \[\operatorname{Inv}_f(C,n)=\Pr_{x\leftarrow U_n}\bigl[f(C(f(x)))=f(x)\bigr],\] where \(U_n\) is uniform on all length-\(n\) bit strings. Finding any length-\(n\) preimage counts as success; the output need not equal the originally sampled \(x\). The challenge is sampled by applying \(f\) to a uniform input, not by choosing a uniform element of its image.

Circuits are finite directed acyclic graphs of fan-in-two AND and OR gates, fan-in-one NOT gates and constants, with named inputs and outputs. Size counts noninput gates, including constants; no restriction is placed on fan-out. Real size limits mean their integer floors. Every circuit is allowed independently at each input length, including circuits with information built into their wiring and constants. No uniform procedure for generating the attack circuits is required. Deterministic circuits suffice for the displayed average-success bound: a randomized attack is a distribution over such circuits, and averaging cannot exceed their common bound.

Weakness means a fixed inverse-polynomial fraction of the sampled challenges defeats every allowed attacker. Strongness here means that the maximum success of any allowed attacker is negligible: smaller than every fixed inverse power for sufficiently large lengths. The exponent \(b\) is fixed before \(d\). This explicitly uses negligible success against exponential-size circuits; it does not add a separate exponentially small success requirement. Security is measured against the input length of each function itself, on all sufficiently large lengths. Both functions are length-preserving, following the source's stated convention; arbitrary padding is not assumed to preserve exponential hardness.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this implication, or a proof of its negation. A positive answer may use an arbitrary construction or existence argument and need not preserve the original security exponent. It must produce a single polynomial-time function with a positive linear exponential attack-size exponent and negligible inversion success. A negative answer must refute the existence implication itself; a barrier for black-box transformations or for a restricted amplification method is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The reverse implication is immediate: negligible inversion success also leaves an inverse-polynomial fraction of inputs hard. The substantive question is the weak-to-strong direction. It does not ask to prove that one-way functions exist without assumptions.

The usual direct-product amplification evaluates the weak function on many independent blocks. Its enlarged input length can turn exponential security in a block length into only stretched-exponential security in the new length. The 2025 revision explicitly identifies this loss as the unresolved issue.

Security-preserving amplification is known under regularity assumptions: at a fixed input length, every value in the image of a regular function has the same number of preimages. The present premise includes arbitrary functions with unequal fiber sizes, so that special case does not establish the general implication.

The question is about existence of a suitable strong function. It does not demand a black-box reduction, restrict forward computation to constant depth, or require the new function to use the same input length as a single invocation of the old one. Its exponential guarantee is nevertheless measured in its own full input length.
